milestone: Milestone 4 - Scientific Communication: Paper and Talk
topic: Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) Analysis Methods: Trustworthiness, Tradeoffs, and Critical Evaluation

entries.objective: Clarify the taxonomy of WCET analysis methods before building the later milestones and final paper.
entries.prompt: Explain the taxonomy of WCET analysis methods in a way suitable for a technical seminar. Separate static, measurement-based, and hybrid methods, and then explain how the deterministic and probabilistic variants lead to SDTA, SPTA, MBDTA, MBPTA, HYDTA, and HYPTA. Focus on assumptions, guarantees, and failure modes rather than producing polished prose.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI response organized the WCET method families into static, measurement-based, and hybrid approaches, with deterministic and probabilistic variants. It helped identify the six method labels and connect them to assumptions such as hardware timing models, test coverage, and statistical validity.

actions: Checked the method names and categories against the assigned WCET reference material.
Compared the AI taxonomy with the milestone notes to make sure deterministic/probabilistic and static/measurement/hybrid dimensions were not mixed.
Rejected any wording that implied measurement-based methods can guarantee the real worst case without qualification.

issues: The first response was too explanatory for milestone style and had to be shortened.
Some statements needed more careful wording because WCET methods differ in the kind of evidence they provide.

integration.section: Milestone 1 background; final paper method overview

entries.reflection: This interaction helped me understand that the central structure is not just three method families, but a two-dimensional classification: analysis basis and type of guarantee. This made the later comparison tables easier to justify.

entries.objective: Place WCET analysis in the wider scientific and engineering context for Milestone 2.
entries.prompt: Create a structured context map for WCET analysis. Do not write a classical related-work section. Instead, show how WCET connects to real-time scheduling, response-time analysis, formal methods, processor architecture, safety certification, and tool support. For each neighboring area, state the connection to WCET and why it matters for embedded systems.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed a context map linking WCET to scheduling, formal verification, architecture, safety standards, and tool support. It also suggested neighboring concepts such as WCRT, abstract interpretation, time-triggered architectures, resource isolation, EVT, runtime monitoring, and ML-based execution-time prediction.

actions: Checked whether each neighboring concept had a real technical connection to WCET rather than being only loosely related.
Kept WCRT because it uses WCET as an input for task-set timing analysis.
Kept abstract interpretation because it is directly connected to static timing analysis.
Separated runtime monitoring and machine learning prediction from WCET evidence because they cannot replace offline WCET guarantees.

issues: Some relationships were initially phrased too broadly and were rewritten as concise notes.
The output was converted into tables to match the milestone requirement against publication-style prose.

integration.section: Milestone 2: context map and related approaches

entries.reflection: This changed my understanding of related work. I realized that the task was not to collect random papers, but to show where WCET sits between scheduling theory, hardware timing behavior, and certification evidence.

entries.objective: Develop the engineering tradeoff analysis for WCET method families.
entries.prompt: Build a tradeoff matrix for the six WCET method families. Compare them using engineering criteria: formal guarantee versus practical deployability, precision versus analysis cost, single-core versus multicore scalability, offline analysis versus online behavior, and certification evidence versus research maturity. For each method, include a short trust note explaining when the method is credible and when its assumptions weaken.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI produced a comparison structure that separated usefulness, cost or weakness, and trustworthiness. It helped frame SDTA as strong but model-dependent, MBDTA as practical but coverage-dependent, HYDTA as a coverage improvement with hardware-state limitations, and MBPTA as promising but certification-challenged.

actions: Compared the tradeoff categories with the milestone checklist requirements.
Checked that the tradeoffs were engineering-relevant rather than purely rhetorical.
Reviewed whether the multicore and certification claims were presented as limitations, not as absolute impossibilities.
Adjusted wording where AI initially made MBPTA sound more mature than current industrial use supports.

issues: The AI tended to make clean contrasts that needed softer wording because real tool choice depends on the target platform.
Some claims about certification maturity required cautious wording.

integration.section: Milestone 2: method-family tradeoff table; final paper tradeoff section

entries.reflection: The main insight was that WCET method selection is not a ranking problem. It is an assumptions problem: the best method is the one whose assumptions are valid for the processor, software, and certification context.

entries.objective: Move from explanation to critical evaluation for Milestone 3.
entries.prompt: Act as a critical reviewer of WCET analysis methods. Identify strengths, limitations, restrictive assumptions, scalability implications, and realistic application boundaries for SDTA, MBDTA, HYDTA, SPTA, MBPTA, and HYPTA. Do not simply say whether a method is good or bad. For each method, explain under which assumptions it works, where those assumptions break down, and which embedded-system examples are suitable or unsuitable.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI helped organize the critical evaluation into strengths, risks, restrictive assumptions, scalability, suitable use cases, unsuitable use cases, and open research questions. The most useful output was the 'assumption versus breakdown condition' structure.

actions: Checked that each criticism was connected to a concrete assumption such as hardware-model correctness, input coverage, or statistical independence.
Removed overly general claims and replaced them with conditional statements.
Compared the suitable and unsuitable examples with the earlier context and tradeoff analysis.
Ensured that the final judgement did not present one WCET method as universally superior.

issues: The first version sounded too much like a finished paper, so it was converted into tables and bullet points.
Some examples needed to be made more specific to embedded systems.

entries.reflection: This interaction helped me separate technical description from scientific judgement. I learned to evaluate each method by asking which evidence it requires, which assumptions it makes, and what happens when those assumptions fail.

entries.objective: Revise Milestones 2 and 3 to comply with the instruction that early milestones should not be publication-style prose.
entries.prompt: Rewrite my Milestone 2 and Milestone 3 material so that it fits the milestone requirements. Avoid publication-style prose. Use bullet points, concise technical statements, comparison tables, structured notes, and explicit assumptions. Keep the scientific content, but make it look like a working technical analysis artifact rather than a polished final paper.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI transformed the earlier paper-like Milestone 2 and Milestone 3 drafts into structured notes. It emphasized tables, engineering tradeoffs, feedback questions, suitability examples, and assumption-breakdown analysis.

actions: Compared the revised structure against the milestone checklist provided by the course.
Checked that the technical content from the earlier drafts was retained.
Reviewed whether the revisions reduced rhetorical polish and increased evidence of stepwise reasoning.
Manually inspected the final PDFs for formatting, table readability, and consistency.

issues: Some formatting details such as spacing around technical notation still needed manual correction.
The revision had to balance natural student style with enough technical precision.

integration.section: Milestone 2 and Milestone 3 complete revised submissions

entries.reflection: This was important because the milestone instructions explicitly asked for scientific reasoning rather than final-paper prose. The revision made the work more transparent: the reader can see the comparison logic, assumptions, and judgement steps.

entries.objective: Synthesize the earlier milestones into the final scientific communication artifact for Milestone 4.
entries.prompt: Using Milestones 1, 2, and 3 as source material, create a professional seminar-paper draft and a 10-minute talk outline. The final paper should not merely concatenate the milestones. It should synthesize the technical contribution, scientific context, tradeoff analysis, critical evaluation, and application discussion into a coherent argument. Preserve citations and separate established claims from my own critical judgement.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI generated a final paper structure with abstract, introduction, method overview, scientific context, tradeoff analysis, critical evaluation, application discussion, open problems, conclusion, references, and AI usage statement. It also produced a short talk outline.

actions: Checked that the final paper reused the reasoning from all three milestones rather than introducing unrelated claims.
Reviewed the argument flow from technical problem to method comparison to critical judgement.
Checked that the final paper did not overstate MBPTA certification readiness.
Confirmed that the talk outline emphasized core idea, tradeoffs, and critical assessment rather than repeating the paper section by section.

issues: Some sentences were too polished and required manual simplification to sound like student-authored scientific writing.
The final paper still required careful checking of citations and formatting before submission.

integration.section: Milestone 4 final paper and talk outline

entries.reflection: This interaction helped turn the milestone artifacts into scientific communication. The main synthesis decision was to make trustworthiness the central theme, because it connects the method taxonomy, tradeoffs, assumptions, certification issues, and open problems.

entries.objective: Check the final argument for unsupported claims, overstatement, and weak scientific positioning.
entries.prompt: Review the final WCET paper draft as a critical examiner. Identify claims that are too strong, insufficiently supported, or unclear. Pay special attention to statements about multicore processors, MBPTA, certification, safety standards, and AI-enabled embedded systems. Suggest wording that is precise but not exaggerated.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI suggested using conditional language for certification and multicore claims. It recommended framing the conclusion around validity of assumptions instead of declaring a single best method.

actions: Manually checked the final judgement against the method comparison tables from Milestones 2 and 3.
Softened absolute wording where the evidence only supported a conditional claim.
Kept unresolved or open issues clearly marked as research challenges rather than solved facts.
Ensured that AI-related timing was presented as an open research direction, not a fully covered topic.

issues: The review step was useful mainly for cautious wording, not for adding new content.
Some suggestions were too conservative and were not all adopted.

integration.section: Final paper conclusion, open research questions, and AI usage statement

entries.reflection: The verification pass improved the scientific tone. I learned that a strong paper does not need to make absolute claims; it is more credible when it states conditions, assumptions, and remaining uncertainty clearly.
